name: POPPY
question: Does individualized one-to-one pelvic floor muscle training reduce symptoms in women with newly diagnosed stage I to III prolapse compared with a lifestyle advice leaflet?

design.blinding: Outcome assessors, gynecologist examiners and statistician masked; participants and physiotherapists not

arms.label: Individualized pelvic floor muscle training (five one-to-one physiotherapy appointments over 16 weeks) plus lifestyle advice leaflet

design.population: 447 treatment-naive women with newly diagnosed, symptomatic stage I to III prolapse of any compartment, recruited at 25 gynecology outpatient centers in the UK, New Zealand and Australia.
design.description: Multicenter, parallel-group, assessor-masked randomized superiority trial
design.locator: PubMed abstract; accepted manuscript PDF pp4,6-9

verdictNote: POP-Q stage improvement at 6 months was not significant; only 66% returned 12-month questionnaires.
takeaway: In 447 women with symptomatic stage I to III prolapse, five one-to-one sessions of individualized pelvic floor muscle training over 16 weeks reduced prolapse symptoms more than a lifestyle advice leaflet alone at 12 months (adjusted POP-SS difference 1.52 points on a 28-point scale).

reports.label: Initial report (12 months)
reports.citation: Hagen S, Stark D, Glazener C, et al. "Individualised Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women With Pelvic Organ Prolapse (POPPY): A Multicentre Randomised Controlled Trial." *Lancet.* 2014;383(9919):796-806. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(13)61977-7
reports.followUp: 12 months from trial entry (blinded POP-Q examination at 6 months)
reports.followUpLocator: PubMed abstract; accepted manuscript PDF p8

results.measure: Mean reduction in POP-SS from baseline at 12 months (0-28 scale); adjusted between-group difference in change
results.note: Linear mixed-effects model adjusted for baseline POP-SS and minimization variables, intention to treat; 295 of 447 women returned 12-month questionnaires. Multiple imputation gave a 12-month difference of 1.66 (95% CI 0.74 to 2.58).
results.locator: PubMed abstract; Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p30, Table 3; p13

results.measure: Mean reduction in POP-SS from baseline at 6 months; adjusted between-group difference in change
results.note: Same linear mixed-effects model as the primary analysis.
results.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p30, Table 3; p13

results.measure: Any further prolapse treatment reported by 12 months (surgery, pessary, physiotherapy referral, estrogen or other)
results.note: Risk difference in percentage points, control minus PFMT; risk ratio 2.1 (95% CI 1.5 to 2.9) for control versus PFMT. Denominators are women who answered the question.
results.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p34, Table 5; p14

results.measure: Less severe POP-Q stage at 6 months (ordinal odds ratio, blinded examination); improvement by one or more stages
results.note: Risk difference for stage improvement 7.5% (95% CI -1.4 to 16.4; P=0.10). POP-Q examinations were available for 168 of 225 and 171 of 222 women; the authors state the trial was not powered for this endpoint.
results.locator: PubMed abstract; Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF pp13,34, Table 5; p19

results.measure: Prolapse reported as 'better' than at study start, 12 months
results.note: Risk difference in percentage points; Mann-Whitney P=0.0125 across better, same and worse categories.
results.locator: Accepted manuscript abstract PDF p4; Table 3 PDF p30

results.measure: Prolapse reported as 'better' than at study start, 6 months
results.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p13; Table 3 PDF p30

results.note: Surgery uptake was similar in the two groups.
results.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p34, Table 5; p14

harms.label: Adverse events reported by participants

values.pfmt: 9 events in the intervention group (8 adverse events, 1 unexpected serious adverse event)

harms.locator: PubMed abstract; Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p12
harms.note: Eight adverse events (6 vaginal symptoms, 1 back pain, 1 abdominal pain) and one unexpected serious adverse event (a skiing injury); none was judged related to the intervention or to trial participation.

harms.label: Discontinued intervention because PFMT was thought to worsen symptoms
harms.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p36, Figure 1
harms.note: 30 women discontinued the intervention in total; the other reasons were lack of time (7), missed appointments or unable to contact (7), post-randomization ineligibility (5), referral for gynecology or surgery (5), travel difficulty (3) and declining the 12-month questionnaire (1).

delivery.label: Intervention schedule
delivery.value: Five one-to-one appointments with a women's health physiotherapist over 16 weeks, at weeks 0, 2, 6, 11 and 16.

delivery.label: Intervention content
delivery.value: Internal pelvic floor muscle assessment (PERFECT scheme) at the first appointment; individualized home program aiming for ten 10-second maximal holds and up to 50 fast contractions three times a day, recorded in a diary; pre-contraction against increased abdominal pressure ('the knack'). Electromyographic or pressure biofeedback and electrical stimulation were not permitted.

delivery.label: Control
delivery.value: Lifestyle advice leaflet (weight loss, constipation, heavy lifting, coughing, high-impact exercise) with no pelvic floor exercise information, posted to control women and handed to intervention women at the first appointment; gynecologic review at 6 months for both groups.

delivery.label: Attendance
delivery.value: 80% (178/222) of the intervention group attended 4 or 5 of the 5 appointments; 70% (156/222) attended all five and 4.5% (10/222) attended none.
delivery.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p12; Table 2 PDF p29

delivery.label: Appointment time and uptake
delivery.value: The first appointment took 80 minutes (60 minutes face to face plus 20 minutes of administration) and follow-up appointments 40 minutes; women attended a mean of 4.2 of 5 appointments.

delivery.label: Exercise performance at 12 months
delivery.note: Performed pelvic floor exercises in the last 4 weeks; risk difference 9.4% (95% CI -0.8 to 19.6; P=0.07).

delivery.label: Other prolapse treatment by 12 months
delivery.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p34, Table 5

delivery.label: Net cost of the intervention
delivery.value: GBP 131.61 per woman (physiotherapy cost GBP 170.24 less GBP 38.63 lower mean cost of subsequent treatment); GBP 86.59 per one-point POP-SS improvement.
delivery.note: Within-trial NHS cost analysis at 12 months, 2009 prices.

delivery.label: Recruitment and follow-up
delivery.value: 2,093 women assessed; 447 randomized (225 versus 222). Questionnaire return was 84% (377/447) at 6 months and 66% (295/447) at 12 months.
delivery.locator: PubMed abstract; Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF pp11,36, Figure 1

delivery.label: Sample size
delivery.value: Target 506 (253 per group) for 80% power to detect a 2.5-point POP-SS difference assuming a standard deviation of 8; 88% of the target was randomized.

delivery.label: Baseline prolapse
delivery.value: Stage II in 75.6% (338/447), of whom 243 were at or below the hymen; combined anterior, posterior and upper-compartment prolapse in 45.4% (202/445); median symptom duration 12 months.
delivery.locator: Accepted manuscript (Aberdeen AURA) PDF p12; Table 1 PDF p27

reports.label: Record-linkage follow-up to 11 years
reports.citation: Fenocchi L, Best C, Mason H, et al. "Long-term effects and costs of pelvic floor muscle training for prolapse: trial follow-up record-linkage study." *Int Urogynecol J.* 2023;34(1):239-246. doi:10.1007/s00192-022-05272-9
reports.followUp: Up to 10 years 9 months (September 2007 to May 2018), Scottish participants

results.measure: Any related secondary-care treatment for a pelvic floor disorder during follow-up (adjusted odds ratio, mixed-effects logistic regression)
results.note: Primary outcome of the record-linkage report, not a prespecified endpoint of the original trial. Authors' absolute risk reduction 9% and number needed to treat 11. Adjusted for baseline POP-SS, prolapse stage, attitude to surgery and age group, with centre as a random effect.
results.locator: PMC9834099 Abstract; Results, women receiving treatment during follow-up

results.measure: Time to first related secondary-care treatment (Cox regression, hazard ratio)
results.note: 264 women and 125 events; adjusted for baseline POP-SS, stage, age group and BMI.
results.locator: PMC9834099 Results, analysis of time to first treatment; Table 5

results.measure: Hospital outpatient and inpatient costs for procedures of interest, 2007 to 2018
results.note: The authors found no clear difference in resource-use costs between groups at 11 years; 109 inpatient episodes of care occurred in 94 women (46 PFMT, 48 control).
results.locator: PMC9834099 Abstract; Results, economic assessment; Table 6

delivery.label: Linked cohort
delivery.value: Linked follow-up data were available for 293 of the 447 original participants (65.5%): 149 in the PFMT group and 144 in the control group.

delivery.label: Outcome definition
delivery.value: Any outpatient or inpatient record with an OPCS-4 procedure code of P18, P22-P24, P26, Q07-Q08, Q54, M51-M58, A70 or H57, or a prespecified ICD-10 diagnosis code. The codes include pessary insertion or removal (P26) and vaginal tape operations for incontinence; most coded inpatient procedures were colporrhaphy or vaginal wall repair (P22, P23, P24, Q54).
delivery.locator: PMC9834099 Methods, analysis dataset; Table 1; Results, economic assessment
